opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty was that, at that time, there simply weren't good tasks for what we wanted to study. When I started working on ReAct, around 2022, most NLP benchmarks were things like question answering, classification, or translation. You give the model an input and it produces an output in one shot. There's no environment, no interaction, no notion of taking an action and getting feedback. So if you want to study an agent that reasons and acts, you're immediately stuck: where does the agent act?

On the other side, reinforcement learning had plenty of interactive environments, like Atari games and simulated robotics. But those weren't language-based, so they didn't really let you test whether a language model's reasoning could help. There was a gap between the two worlds, and the task had to sit somewhere in that gap.

So I spent a lot of time asking what kind of task is both interactive and requires real language reasoning, while still being simple enough to evaluate cleanly. That's partly why we ended up with things like multi-hop question answering using a Wikipedia API, where the model has to search, look things up, and decide what to do next, and also text-based environments like ALFWorld and WebShop, where the agent has to act in a world described in language.

There's a deeper reason it was hard, too. In research, people often think the method is the main contribution, but the choice of task actually defines what problem you're solving. If you choose a task that's too easy or too artificial, even a good idea looks trivial. If it's too hard, nothing works, and you can't tell whether the idea is right. And because agents were such a new direction, there was no community consensus on what the "right" benchmark was. You weren't just solving a problem; you were also trying to define what the problem is.

Looking back, I think that's one of the most important lessons I took from that period: in a new area, choosing or building the task is often harder and more important than designing the method. A good task tells you what matters. Later work like WebShop, and benchmarks for agents more broadly, came partly from that feeling that we need better tasks before we can make real progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes the lack of suitable interactive, language-based tasks, but does not say the challenge was finding tasks that demonstrated ReAct’s promise within the capabilities of then-available models such as GPT-3 or PaLM.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think choosing tasks was the hardest part of the whole project, much harder than the method itself.

The idea of ReAct is actually very simple: you let the model think, then act, then observe, and loop. Once you see it, it feels almost obvious. But in 2022, when we started, there was no agent benchmark. There was no "here is the standard task for testing a language model that acts in an environment." So the question became: what task do you pick where reasoning alone isn't enough, acting alone isn't enough, but combining them actually matters?

That's a very narrow target. If you pick something like a pure QA benchmark, the model can just answer from memory, and action doesn't help. If you pick a pure control task, like a game, then the "thinking" part looks decorative, and reviewers will say you just added some text. You need a task where the model genuinely has to go look something up, check what came back, adjust its plan, and the trace of reasoning has to visibly change what it does next.

So we spent a lot of time just searching. We ended up with HotpotQA and FEVER with a Wikipedia API, because multi-hop questions force you to retrieve, read, and then decide what to retrieve next. And then ALFWorld and WebShop on the decision-making side, because those are environments where you can see the model get stuck without reasoning, and recover with it. That combination was deliberate: one side shows reasoning helps acting, the other shows acting helps reasoning.

The other difficulty was infrastructure. At the time, almost nobody was building tool environments for language models. You had to write the wrapper, define the action space, decide what an observation looks like as text, handle all the edge cases. That's not glamorous work, and a lot of the effort of the paper went into it rather than into anything algorithmic.

Looking back, I think that experience is why I later got so interested in building environments and benchmarks like SWE-bench and tau-bench. The lesson from ReAct was that in the agent setting, the task often is the research contribution. The method is simple; what's hard is finding the right problem that makes the method's value legible.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing tasks where reasoning and acting both matter and notes that no agent benchmark existed in 2022. It does not say the tasks had to fit the capabilities of then-available models such as GPT-3 or PaLM.

astra-6.text:
The difficulty was finding tasks where reasoning and action both really mattered. If you choose a task that can be solved just by thinking, you don’t demonstrate why interaction with an environment is useful. And if you choose a task that only requires a few straightforward actions, you don’t demonstrate why reasoning is useful.

So we wanted tasks where the two were interdependent: you reason about what to do, take an action, get new information, and then revise your reasoning. There’s also a practical challenge: when an agent fails, is the task beyond the model’s capabilities, or is the method not helping? You need tasks that are challenging enough to reveal the benefit, but still within reach so you can actually study that interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks should reveal the method’s benefit while remaining “within reach,” but it does not identify that reach in relation to the capabilities of then-available models such as GPT-3 or PaLM.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge was finding tasks where reasoning and acting both really mattered. If a task could be solved just by thinking, you didn’t need interaction with an environment. And if it only required a simple sequence of actions, there wasn’t much reason to add reasoning. We wanted something where you had to act to get new information, then reason about that information to decide what to do next.

There was also a practical research question: how do you demonstrate that this is a general idea rather than a trick for one benchmark? So choosing tasks meant balancing that conceptual fit with having environments where we could run experiments and evaluate the results clearly.

r001.rationale: The response describes selecting tasks where reasoning and action both matter and where experiments can be evaluated, but it does not say the tasks needed to demonstrate ReAct’s promise within the capabilities of then-available models such as GPT-3 or PaLM.
